title: The Protein That Copies Its Own Shape
paragraphs: A ewe in a hill flock begins to rub.
Her gait goes wide, she startles at nothing, and within a few months she is dead.
Shepherds in Britain were describing this pattern by the mid eighteenth century, and they named it for the rubbing: scrapie.
Almost nothing about it looked like an infection: no fever, no swelling, no rise in antibodies, none of the noise a body makes against an intruder.
Under the microscope the brain was riddled with holes, like a sponge.
In the 1930s a simple experiment settled one question and opened a harder one.
Brain material from a sick sheep, injected into healthy sheep, gave them the disease.
Scrapie was transmissible, but whatever was passed behaved like nothing in the microbiology textbooks.
It slipped through filters fine enough to hold back bacteria.
It provoked no immune response at any point.
And it took its time: injected animals stayed well for a year or more before the first symptom.
Then came experiments designed to measure the agent rather than see it.
Radiation damages nucleic acid, so a larger genome offers a larger target.
Scrapie refused to cooperate.
Ultraviolet light at the wavelength nucleic acid absorbs most strongly, at doses that would cut the infectivity of an ordinary virus by a factor of thousands, barely touched it.
Enzymes that cut DNA and RNA did nothing measurable.
The mirror image was just as striking.
Treatments aimed at protein worked.
Proteases lowered the titer.
Set the two results side by side and the conclusion was awkward but plain: whatever carried scrapie between animals was made of protein and carried no nucleic acid at all.
Purification caught up in 1982, when fractions of infected hamster brain were enriched step by step and infectivity tracked with one small protein.
The particle was named prion, from proteinaceous and infectious, and the protein itself PrP.
The gene for PrP had not been smuggled in by the agent.
It sat in the animal's own chromosomes, and healthy uninfected animals transcribed it steadily, hanging the finished protein on the surface of their neurons.
Infected and healthy brain held the same protein, from the same gene, with the same amino acids in the same order.
The difference was shape.
The normal cellular form is soluble, sits on the cell surface, is digested to nothing by a protease within minutes, and is roughly forty percent alpha helix with almost no beta sheet.
The disease form is insoluble, gathers into clumps and long fibrils, and runs near thirty percent helix with more than forty percent sheet.

Give it a protease and it does not disappear: the enzyme trims a loose tail and stops, leaving a resistant core of about twenty-seven to thirty kilodaltons out of a protein of thirty-three to thirty-five.
One chain, two folds, two fates.
It is easy, looking back, to tell this as a story about a stubborn establishment and a lone heretic, and that telling is unfair.
The objection was not fussiness.
Biology had spent thirty years establishing that heredity lives in sequence, copied by base pairing, and that protein is the end of the line.
An infectious protein with no genome was not a small amendment: it asked for a second channel of heredity, one in which the thing copied was not a message at all.
Demanding extraordinary evidence for that was the correct first response, and the evidence took twenty years to assemble.
What made the idea thinkable was a mechanism that copies no message.
The misfolded form is not a poison.
It is a mold.
A molecule already folded the wrong way binds a normal one, holds it against its own sheet face, and presses it into the same geometry.
The new convert is a mold in its turn.
Molecules stack into a fibril that grows at both ends, and when a fibril snaps, one growing surface becomes two.
That mechanism also explains the strange clock.
The slow part is the beginning, the improbable first seed, whether it arrives by injection or forms on its own in one cell out of billions.
Once enough seeds exist the curve turns steep and the brain fills quickly, which is why these diseases seem to arrive all at once after years of nothing.
In kuru, a human prion disease, some incubation periods ran past forty years.
The sharpest objection to the protein idea was never the sequence rule.
It was strains.
Isolates of scrapie taken from different sources and passaged in mice bred to be genetically identical behaved as distinct and stable varieties.
One strain killed at about 150 days and another at more than 300, reproducibly, in the same inbred line.
Each left its own signature map of which brain regions turned spongy and which were spared.
A strain bred true through passage after passage.
That is inheritance of a trait, and inheritance by an agent with no genes looked like a contradiction.
The resolution is that the shape carries the trait.
A given strain is a particular fold, a particular way the sheet is stacked, and each fold templates that arrangement onto the next molecule.
The information is real and heritable.
It is simply written in geometry rather than in bases.
Crossing between species revealed a second property.
Put a hamster prion into a mouse and most animals stay well, while the few that sicken take far longer than a mouse given a mouse prion.
Pass the agent again, now mouse to mouse, and the incubation shortens and settles at a new stable value.
The obstacle is real, but it is a steep hill rather than a wall, and it belongs to a pair rather than a species: what matters is the fit between the incoming shape and the host's own sequence.
Two episodes showed how partial that protection is.
Cattle in Britain developed a spongiform disease recognized in 1986 and traced to feed containing rendered tissue from other ruminants.
Ten years later a new human disease appeared in people who had eaten beef, and fewer than two hundred died of it in Britain.
Kuru had spread decades earlier among the Fore of Papua New Guinea through mortuary practices in which the dead were eaten, and faded once those stopped.
Hospitals inherited a practical problem.
Sterilization protocols destroy nucleic acid and unfold ordinary proteins.
A prion offers nothing of the first kind and is far too stable for the second.
A standard autoclave cycle, 121 degrees Celsius for fifteen minutes, does not reliably do it.

Published guidance calls instead for 134 degrees for eighteen minutes in a porous load autoclave, or an hour in one molar sodium hydroxide, or an hour in bleach at twenty thousand parts per million available chlorine.
Worse, the reagents that usually make a specimen safe do the opposite here.
Formaldehyde fixes the tissue, hardening it and sealing the infectivity inside, where it survives for years, and alcohol behaves much the same way.
Instruments have carried infectivity through ordinary cleaning, so high risk work leans on single use tools.
For a long time this looked like one bizarre corner of pathology.
That has changed.
The same templating move turns up across a set of proteins with no relation to PrP.
Alpha synuclein in Parkinson disease, tau in Alzheimer disease, amyloid beta, and the polyglutamine tracts of Huntington disease all misfold into sheet rich aggregates that seed more of themselves.
Inject affected brain extract into a healthy animal and matching deposits appear, then spread along connected circuits.
Two cautions attach to that list.
The word infectious is doing much less work there than it appears.

Nothing indicates that Alzheimer disease or Parkinson disease passes between people in ordinary life, and treating a shared molecular move as evidence of contagion is the error the field works hardest to avoid.
The second caution runs the other way: self templating is not only a failure.
Yeast carry protein based traits with no change to any gene, and a few animal proteins in memory and immune signaling switch on this way.
The sheep disease that broke the rules in the eighteenth century was the first visible case of something ordinary.
Many chains can fold more than one way, and one of those ways can copy itself.

questions.stem: According to the passage, applying a protease to the disease form of PrP leaves behind
choices: nothing, since the enzyme digests it completely
a soluble fragment that can no longer join a fibril
a resistant core of about twenty-seven to thirty kilodaltons
a fragment of thirty-three to thirty-five kilodaltons, the full length protein
a stretch that is roughly forty percent alpha helix

proof.quote: leaving a resistant core of about twenty-seven to thirty kilodaltons

questions.why: Paragraph 6 states it directly: the enzyme trims a loose tail and stops, leaving a resistant core of about twenty-seven to thirty kilodaltons. That paragraph carries several numbers, so the trick is matching the right one to the right thing.
distractorNotes: Complete digestion is what happens to the normal cellular form in paragraph 6, not to the disease form.
Solubility belongs to the normal form, while the disease form stays insoluble and keeps gathering into fibrils.
Thirty-three to thirty-five kilodaltons is the size of the whole protein before the enzyme trims it, not what survives.
Forty percent helix describes the normal fold in paragraph 6, and it is a structural figure rather than a fragment.

questions.stem: The passage reports that ultraviolet light tuned to the wavelength nucleic acid takes up best
choices: destroyed scrapie infectivity at low doses
left scrapie infectivity nearly untouched
was never actually tested on scrapie
reduced scrapie infectivity by a factor of thousands
worked only when combined with enzymes that cut DNA and RNA

proof.quote: barely touched it
at doses that would cut the infectivity of an ordinary virus by a factor of thousands

questions.why: Paragraph 3 says that doses high enough to cut an ordinary virus by a factor of thousands barely touched scrapie. That survival is the whole point of the experiment, since it argued against a nucleic acid genome.
distractorNotes: Low doses did nothing and high doses did little more, which is the opposite of what this choice claims.
Paragraph 3 describes that test being run, and its result is what pushed the field toward a protein.
A drop of that size is what the same dose did to an ordinary virus, which is the comparison the paragraph draws.
Enzymes that cut DNA and RNA had no measurable effect either, so pairing them changes nothing.

questions.stem: Which treatment does the passage name as part of published guidance for prion contaminated instruments?
choices: an autoclave cycle at 121 degrees for fifteen minutes
an hour in formaldehyde followed by alcohol
eighteen minutes at 134 degrees in a porous load autoclave
twenty minutes in bleach at two hundred parts per million chlorine
several rounds of ordinary cleaning between uses

proof.quote: 134 degrees for eighteen minutes in a porous load autoclave
does not reliably do it

questions.why: Paragraph 14 lists the accepted options, and 134 degrees for eighteen minutes in a porous load autoclave is the first of them. The others in that list are sodium hydroxide and much stronger bleach.
distractorNotes: That is the standard cycle paragraph 14 names as the one that does not reliably work.
Formaldehyde and alcohol are named as making things worse, since they fix the tissue and seal infectivity inside.
The bleach figure in paragraph 14 is twenty thousand parts per million for a full hour, far stronger and far longer.
Paragraph 14 says instruments have carried infectivity through ordinary cleaning, so that is the problem rather than the solution.

questions.stem: According to the passage, one feature that made scrapie unlike a familiar infection was that it
choices: produced a high fever within days
could not be transmitted by injection
was visible under an ordinary light microscope
was held back by filters that stop bacteria
provoked no immune response at any point

proof.quote: It provoked no immune response at any point.
It slipped through filters fine enough to hold back bacteria.

questions.why: Paragraph 2 lists the oddities, and the absence of any immune response is one of them. Paragraph 1 makes the same point from the clinical side, noting no fever, no swelling, and no rise in antibodies.
distractorNotes: Paragraph 1 lists the absence of fever among the things that made scrapie look unlike an infection.
Injection of brain material did transmit it, which is the finding paragraph 2 opens with.
The agent was never seen, and paragraph 3 says the experiments were designed to measure it rather than to see it.
It slipped through those filters, which is how investigators knew it was smaller than bacteria.

questions.stem: The evidence from scrapie strains passaged in genetically identical mice included
choices: different incubation periods and different damage maps
different amino acid sequences in the host protein
a steady loss of infectivity with each passage
the appearance of new genes in the mouse genome
identical incubation periods in every case once the host line was inbred

proof.quote: One strain killed at about 150 days and another at more than 300
Each left its own signature map of which brain regions turned spongy

questions.why: Paragraph 10 gives both signatures: one strain killing near 150 days and another past 300 in the same inbred line, and each strain leaving its own map of which brain regions turned spongy.
distractorNotes: The host protein sequence was the same in every mouse, which is exactly what made the result so puzzling.
Strains bred true through passage after passage rather than fading out.
No genetic change in the mice was involved, since the whole point was that the mice were identical.
The strains differed sharply in incubation, by more than a hundred fifty days in the example given.

questions.stem: As used in paragraph 10, "strains" most nearly means
choices: forces that stretch or deform a molecule
efforts made under difficult conditions
versions of the agent whose properties reproduce reliably
lines of laboratory mice bred over generations to be genetically identical
samples taken from a single infected animal

proof.quote: behaved as distinct and stable varieties
A strain bred true through passage after passage.

questions.why: Paragraph 10 defines the word by what it describes: isolates that behave as distinct and stable varieties, each with its own incubation period and its own pattern of damage, holding true through passage after passage.
distractorNotes: That is a mechanical sense of the word, and the paragraph is describing varieties of an agent rather than forces on a molecule.
The everyday sense does not fit a sentence about isolates that reproduce their own properties reliably.
The inbred mice are the background the comparison was run in, not what the word names.
A single sample could contain any variety, so this names the act of collecting rather than the behavior being described.

questions.stem: As used in paragraph 14, "fixes" most nearly means
choices: repairs damage done to the tissue
settles on one value something that had been variable
attaches the specimen to a slide
hardens and preserves the tissue chemically
removes the infectious material from the tissue

proof.quote: fixes the tissue, hardening it and sealing the infectivity inside

questions.why: The same sentence in paragraph 14 supplies the meaning: formaldehyde hardens the tissue and seals the infectivity inside, where it survives for years. The word describes chemical preservation, not repair.
distractorNotes: Repair is the everyday sense, and the paragraph is describing a treatment that makes the hazard worse rather than better.
That sense of the word belongs to prices and schedules, not to what formaldehyde does to a specimen.
Mounting is a real laboratory step, but the sentence is about hardening tissue and trapping what is inside it.
The sentence says the reverse: the infectivity survives for years inside the treated tissue.

questions.stem: The account of incubation in paragraph 9 most strongly suggests that
choices: symptoms track how much conversion has occurred, not time since exposure
the agent lies dormant until a fever activates it
younger animals incubate the disease longer than older ones do
most exposed animals never accumulate any misfolded protein
the immune system holds the agent in check for many years before it finally fails

proof.quote: The slow part is the beginning, the improbable first seed
Once enough seeds exist the curve turns steep and the brain fills quickly

questions.why: Paragraph 9 says the slow step is forming the improbable first seed, and that once enough seeds exist the curve turns steep and the brain fills quickly. Timing therefore follows the amount of templating, which is why the disease seems to arrive all at once.
distractorNotes: No fever appears anywhere in this passage, and paragraph 1 lists its absence as one of the original puzzles.
Age is never raised as a variable in the account of incubation.
Paragraph 9 says the first seed is improbable, not that seeding usually fails outright.
Paragraph 2 says the agent provokes no immune response at all, so there is nothing holding it in check.

questions.stem: Based on paragraph 12, which step would most likely shorten the incubation period of a prion in a new host species?
choices: raising the dose of the first inoculation until every animal sickens
passing the agent through several generations of that host
using a host whose own PrP gene has been deleted
selecting a strain that has never been passaged before
storing the inoculum at a lower temperature before use

proof.quote: Pass the agent again, now mouse to mouse, and the incubation shortens

questions.why: Paragraph 12 describes exactly this: pass the agent again in the new host and the incubation shortens and settles at a new stable value. The shape adapts to the host sequence it is now copying itself onto.
distractorNotes: Dose is not the variable paragraph 12 identifies, since the shortening comes with repeated passage in the new host.
A host with no PrP of its own would supply nothing for the template to convert, which is the reverse of what is wanted.
Being new to the host is what makes a first passage long, so an unpassaged strain would not help.
Storage conditions of the inoculum are never mentioned as affecting incubation.

questions.stem: The central point of the passage is that
choices: scrapie has been recognized in British sheep since the eighteenth century and is still untreatable
sterilization practice in hospitals has had to change because of prion diseases
a protein can copy information in its shape, and this is not rare
the central dogma of molecular biology has turned out to be false in its essentials
an infectious agent can have strains without any genetic differences

proof.quote: Many chains can fold more than one way, and one of those ways can copy itself.
It is simply written in geometry rather than in bases.
The same templating move turns up across a set of proteins with no relation to PrP.
the first visible case of something ordinary

questions.why: The passage moves from one sheep disease to a general property of proteins, ending in paragraphs 15 and 16 with a list of other proteins that template their own shape and with a normal cellular version of the same trick.
distractorNotes: Scrapie opens the passage as an entry point, and the argument travels well past sheep.
Sterilization gets one paragraph as a practical consequence rather than being the point the passage builds toward.
Paragraph 7 treats the sequence rule as sound and hard won, and the passage adds a second channel rather than overturning the first.
Strains are one striking piece of evidence in paragraph 10, offered in support of the larger claim rather than as the claim.

questions.stem: Paragraph 13 is included mainly in order to
choices: show that the species barrier can be crossed under real conditions
argue that beef is unsafe to eat
explain how rendered animal feed is manufactured
date the first recognition of scrapie in Britain
establish that kuru and the cattle disease were caused by the very same strain

proof.quote: Two episodes showed how partial that protection is.
it is a steep hill rather than a wall

questions.why: Paragraph 12 ends by calling the barrier a steep hill rather than a wall, and paragraph 13 supplies two real episodes, cattle in Britain and kuru among the Fore, in which the agent did move. It is evidence for the point just made.
distractorNotes: The paragraph reports a past epidemic and its toll without making any recommendation about what to eat.
Feed is named as the route of spread in a single clause, and the manufacturing process is never described.
That date is in paragraph 1, and paragraph 13 deals entirely with the twentieth century.
The two episodes are presented as separate events in different species, with no claim that one strain caused both.

questions.stem: Which best describes how the passage is organized?
choices: a list of prion diseases followed by their treatments
a debate between two camps, with each given equal space
a chronological history of one laboratory's work
a practical guide to sterilization, with background supplied first
a puzzle set out, narrowed by evidence, then resolved and widened

proof.quote: settled one question and opened a harder one
the conclusion was awkward but plain
The resolution is that the shape carries the trait.
The same templating move turns up across a set of proteins with no relation to PrP.

questions.why: The passage opens with a disease nothing explained, spends the middle paragraphs eliminating a genome and building a mechanism, then widens in paragraphs 15 and 16 to other proteins that do the same thing.
distractorNotes: Treatments never appear, and the passage offers nothing on curing any of these diseases.
Only one position is developed, and the opposing view in paragraph 7 is explained rather than argued for at length.
No laboratory is followed, and the passage moves across decades, species, and proteins rather than tracking one group.
Sterilization occupies a single paragraph well after the argument is built, and it is a consequence rather than the destination.

questions.stem: The author's attitude toward the scientists who first rejected the idea of an infectious protein is best described as
choices: amused by their confusion
sharply critical of their caution
wholly indifferent to their position
admiring of their eventual conversion
sympathetic to their reasoning

proof.quote: that telling is unfair
Demanding extraordinary evidence for that was the correct first response

questions.why: Paragraph 7 calls the heretic story unfair, says the objection was not fussiness, and ends by calling the demand for extraordinary evidence the correct first response. That is a defense of the doubters.
distractorNotes: Nothing in paragraph 7 treats the objection as confusion, and amusement is not the note the paragraph strikes.
Criticism is what the paragraph sets out to correct, and it calls their caution correct.
Indifference would mean no judgment at all, and the paragraph makes one in its final sentence.
No conversion is described, and the paragraph praises the initial resistance rather than any later change of mind.

questions.stem: In paragraph 16, the author's attitude toward calling Alzheimer disease infectious is best described as
choices: enthusiastic about a bold new framing
uneasy with the word and careful to limit it
confident that the disease will prove contagious
dismissive of the entire line of research as a distraction
neutral, reporting the claim without any comment

proof.quote: The word infectious is doing much less work there than it appears.
treating a shared molecular move as evidence of contagion is the error the field works hardest to avoid

questions.why: Paragraph 16 opens with a caution, says the word is doing much less work there than it appears, and calls the slide from shared mechanism to contagion the error the field works hardest to avoid.
distractorNotes: The paragraph opens with a warning rather than with enthusiasm about the framing.
The author states that nothing indicates these diseases pass between people in ordinary life.
Paragraph 15 treats the seeding work as solid and interesting, so the research itself is not being brushed aside.
Comment is exactly what the paragraph offers, naming the loose use of the word as an error.

questions.stem: The passage supports all of the following statements EXCEPT:
choices: Healthy animals that have never been exposed still make PrP
Formaldehyde treatment can leave infectivity intact for years
The disease form of PrP contains more beta sheet than the normal form
A prion strain carries a short stretch of its own nucleic acid
Breaking a fibril increases the number of surfaces that can convert

proof.quote: healthy uninfected animals transcribed it steadily
sealing the infectivity inside, where it survives for years
almost no beta sheet
more than forty percent sheet
when a fibril snaps, one growing surface becomes two
carried no nucleic acid at all

questions.why: The passage argues the opposite at length: paragraph 3 reports that nucleic acid damaging treatments did not touch the agent, and paragraph 11 says the strain information is written in geometry rather than in bases. The other four statements all sit on the page.
distractorNotes: Paragraph 5 says the gene sits in the animal's own chromosomes and that healthy uninfected animals transcribe it steadily.
Paragraph 14 says formaldehyde hardens the tissue and seals the infectivity inside, where it survives for years.
Paragraph 6 contrasts almost no sheet in the normal fold with more than forty percent in the disease fold.
Paragraph 8 says that when a fibril snaps, one growing surface becomes two.

questions.stem: A reader who wanted to know why a prion takes longer to cause disease the first time it enters a new species should turn to
choices: paragraph 3
paragraph 8
paragraph 10
paragraph 12
paragraph 15

proof.quote: the few that sicken take far longer than a mouse given a mouse prion

questions.why: Paragraph 12 is the one that crosses species: a hamster prion in a mouse, the long and incomplete first passage, and the shortening that follows on later passage in the new host.
distractorNotes: Paragraph 3 is the radiation work that argued against a genome, with no mention of species.
Paragraph 8 gives the templating mechanism in general terms and never brings in a second species.
Paragraph 10 concerns strains within one host species, mice bred to be identical.
Paragraph 15 extends the mechanism to other proteins and does not return to crossing species.
